name: Italian Game
tagline: Bishop to c4, eyes on f7. The oldest opening still played at the top level.

theory.big_idea: White develops the light-squared bishop to its most aggressive diagonal (a2–g8) where it stares at f7. f7 is the weakest point in Black's position because it is defended only by the king. Everything else in the Italian flows from that one bishop: whether White builds a big pawn centre with c3 and d4, sacrifices a pawn to rip open lines, or plays a slow build-up and attacks later.
theory.structure: Symmetrical e-pawns on e4/e5 with pawns still on d2/d7. This is the classic 'Open Game' skeleton. The tension is over whether White gets in d2–d4 under good circumstances. If White does, the position opens and development counts. If Black stops it, the game becomes a slow manoeuvring battle where knight routes decide everything.
white_plans: Play c3 then d4, building the ideal pawn duo on d4+e4 and opening lines while ahead in development.
The modern slow build: d3, O-O, Re1, Nbd2–f1–g3, then h3 and a delayed d4. White keeps the tension for twenty moves and outmanoeuvres Black.
Direct attack on f7 with Ng5 (in the Two Knights) or a pawn sacrifice with b4 (Evans Gambit) to seize the centre by force.
Rook lift Re1–e3–g3 or a kingside pawn storm once Black's counterplay on the queenside is contained.
black_plans: Mirror the setup with ...Bc5, ...d6, ...Nf6, ...O-O and hold the centre; then re-route a knight via ...Ne7–g6 or hit back with ...d5.
Play the sharp ...Nf6 (Two Knights) inviting 4.Ng5 and answering with the Polerio counter-gambit 4...d5 5.exd5 Na5!
Retreat the bishop to a7 in advance so that White's d4 never comes with tempo.
Trade off White's strong Italian bishop with ...Na5 or ...Be6.
traps: The Fried Liver Attack: 3...Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Nxd5?? 6.Nxf7! Kxf7 7.Qf3+ and Black's king is dragged into the open. Black must play 5...Na5!
The Legal Trap pattern: if Black pins with ...Bg4 and grabs too greedily, White can sometimes sacrifice the queen with Nxe5 followed by Bxf7+ and Nd5#.
Blackburne Shilling Trap (Black's trap): 3...Nd4?! 4.Nxe5?? Qg5! 5.Nxf7 Qxg2 6.Rf1 Qxe4+ and White collapses. Correct is 4.Nxd4.
theory.who: Play this if you like clear, natural development and open positions where tactics decide. It teaches you more about basic chess principles than any other opening.

progression.arc: The Italian is where you learn what the opening principles actually mean. Everything you build later stands on this.

stages.goal: Reach a healthy position by move ten without thinking.
learn: The six-move skeleton: e4, Nf3, Bc4, c3, d3, O-O. Play it against anything Black does on move three.
Why Bc4 and not Bb5 or Be2 — the f7 square is defended only by the king, so it is the one target that exists from move one.
The three ways Black can answer 3.Bc4: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco), 3...Nf6 (Two Knights), 3...Be7 (Hungarian). You need a reply to each.
stages.drill: Set the board up and play the six-move skeleton twenty times against a friend or an engine at low strength. Your hands should know it before your head does.
stages.mistake: Playing 4.Ng5 in every position because it 'attacks f7'. It is one idea, not a plan, and a prepared opponent punishes it.
stages.ready: You can play the first eight moves without pausing and explain why each piece went where it did.

stages.goal: Understand the d4 break — when it wins the game and when it throws it away.
learn: The difference between 5.d4 (immediate, opens the game while Black is behind) and 5.d3 (slow, keeps the tension). Modern practice prefers d3.
What happens to the pawn structure after ...exd4 cxd4 — White gets d4+e4 and the c-file, Black gets the d5 square and a target.
Why ...a6 and ...Ba7 exist: Black is removing d4 from your list of good moves before you play it.
stages.drill: Take the main-line position after 8.Nbd2 and write down, in words, three plans for White and three for Black. Then check them against the plans card above.
stages.mistake: Playing d4 the moment it is legal. In the Pianissimo you are supposed to spend eight moves earning it.
stages.ready: You can look at an Italian position and say whether the centre should be opened or kept closed, and why.

stages.goal: Play the middlegame, not just the opening.
learn: The knight tour Nb1–d2–f1–g3 and its cousin ...Nc6–e7–g6. Both sides re-route toward the kingside; whoever finishes first attacks first.
The rook lift Re1–e3–g3 and when the e-file is worth more than the attack.
How to meet ...d5: usually exd5 followed by piece pressure, occasionally e5 gaining space.
stages.drill: Play ten games where you commit to reaching the Pianissimo tabiya and then attacking the kingside. Lose some. Note where the attack ran out of pieces.
stages.mistake: Attacking with two pieces. An attack needs three or four attackers against the defenders present — count before you commit.
stages.ready: You have won a game with the Nf1–g3 manoeuvre and lost one because you attacked too early. Both lessons matter.

stages.goal: Own the sharp branches and the endgames.
learn: The Evans Gambit as a surprise weapon, including the critical defences 5...Ba5, 5...Bc5 and 5...Be7.
The Two Knights in full: the Fried Liver, the Polerio 5...Na5, the Traxler 4...Bc5!?, and the modern 4.d4.
Endgames from the Italian: bishop against knight with pawns on both wings, and how the extra central pawn tells.
stages.drill: Take one Evans Gambit line and analyse it thirty moves deep with an engine, then close the engine and try to explain the evaluation.
stages.mistake: Treating the gambit lines as tricks. At any decent level they are real openings with real theory.
stages.ready: You can play both sides of the Two Knights and you know which side you would rather have.

progression.study: Paul Morphy for the attacking version, Anatoly Karpov and Magnus Carlsen for the modern slow build. Kasparov–Anand, Riga 1995 is the most famous Evans Gambit of the last century.
progression.next: Once the Italian feels automatic, learn the Ruy Lopez. The ideas transfer directly and the Ruy is simply a better version of the same opening.

name: Ruy Lopez (Spanish Game)
tagline: The most respected opening in chess. Slow pressure that never goes away.

theory.big_idea: 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5. The threat is not immediate — after 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5?? Qd4 wins the piece back — but it is a permanent nagging question. White's real plan is to build the centre with c3 and d4 while Black's pieces are tangled defending e5, then manoeuvre the knight to g3 and attack the kingside. It is the opening of long-term positional pressure.
theory.structure: White gets a broad centre with pawns on d4 and e4 supported by c3. Black usually plays ...d6 and ...b5 and then either holds with ...c5 (the Chigorin) or breaks with ...d5 (the Marshall Attack, a whole-pawn gambit). The Exchange Variation produces a completely different structure: Black gets doubled c-pawns but the bishop pair.
white_plans: The Spanish manoeuvre: Nb1–d2–f1–g3 (sometimes on to f5 or h5), the classic slow build-up toward a kingside attack.
Establish the pawn centre with c3 and d4, then decide whether to release the tension with d5 (closing) or dxe5 (opening).
The Exchange Variation: 4.Bxc6 dxc6 wrecks Black's queenside pawn structure. White plays for a winning king-and-pawn endgame from move four.
a4 undermining Black's b5–c6 queenside chain.
black_plans: The Breyer/Chigorin retreat: re-route the knight from c6 to b8–d7 or a5–c4 and slowly untangle.
The Marshall Attack: sacrifice a pawn with ...d5 for a lasting initiative against White's king.
The Berlin Defence: force an early queen trade and head for a slightly worse but extremely tough endgame with the bishop pair. This is the opening that ended Kasparov's title reign.
Break with ...d5 or ...f5 once White's centre is committed.
traps: The Noah's Ark Trap: after an early ...b5 and ...c5, Black's queenside pawns can roll forward and physically trap White's bishop on b3 — ...c4 and ...b5–b4 nets a piece.
Do not play 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Nxe4 6.Re1?! d5 7.Nxe5 — this is the Riga/Open Spanish, sharp and double-edged, not a free piece.
Never grab with 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5?? — 5...Qd4! forks e5 and e4.
theory.who: Play this if you are willing to invest in theory and you enjoy squeezing opponents slowly. It rewards patience and understanding, not memorised tricks.

progression.arc: The Ruy is a five-year opening. You will keep finding new layers in it, which is exactly why every world champion has played it.

stages.goal: Survive the first ten moves and understand why the bishop goes to b5.
learn: The Morphy main line: 3...a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3. Memorise it as one unit.
Why 5.O-O ignores the e4-pawn: after 5...Nxe4 6.d4 the pawn always comes back.
The Exchange Variation 4.Bxc6 as your safety net — it is fully playable and needs almost no theory.
stages.drill: Play the Exchange Variation for a month. It teaches you the structure without the memorisation, and you will win endgames.
stages.mistake: Playing 5.Nxe5 after 4.Bxc6 dxc6. It loses a pawn to 5...Qd4 and it is the single most common Ruy Lopez blunder.
stages.ready: You can reach move nine of the Closed Ruy from memory and you have won a game with the Exchange endgame plan.

stages.goal: Understand the two centres — the tense one and the closed one.
learn: After c3 and d4, the three ways the centre can resolve: d5 (closed, play on the wings), dxe5 (open, piece play), or keeping the tension (usually best).
The Carlsbad-like queenside chain b5–c6–a6 and White's undermining a4.
Why the h3 move is played in almost every line — it stops ...Bg4, which would undermine the defence of d4.
stages.drill: Set up the position after 11.d4 in the Chigorin and play it out against an engine ten times from both sides. Note what changes when White plays d5.
stages.mistake: Releasing the central tension because it feels uncomfortable. Whoever resolves the tension first usually helps the other side.
stages.ready: You can explain what changes about both sides' plans the moment White plays d5.

stages.goal: Learn the manoeuvres that make the Ruy the Ruy.
learn: The Spanish knight tour Nb1–d2–f1–g3 (or e3) — the model for slow attacking build-ups in every opening.
Black's counterplans: the Chigorin ...Na5, the Breyer ...Nb8–d7, the Zaitsev ...Bb7 and ...Re8.
The a4 break and when to take on b5 versus when to leave the tension.
stages.drill: Play twenty games reaching the Closed tabiya and write one sentence after each about where your pieces belonged.
stages.mistake: Rushing the kingside attack. In the Ruy the attack arrives around move twenty-five, not move fifteen.
stages.ready: You can name the square each of your eight pieces wants without looking at a book.

stages.goal: Handle the theoretical branches and the endgames the Ruy produces.
learn: The Berlin Defence and its endgame — you will face it, and knowing how to press without queens is a genuine skill.
The Marshall Attack and your chosen Anti-Marshall (8.a4 or 8.h3), because Black gets a free pawn sacrifice otherwise.
The Noah's Ark Trap and the whole family of positions where the b3-bishop gets short of squares.
stages.drill: Study ten Berlin endgames move by move. It is the least glamorous and most valuable study you will do this year.
stages.mistake: Avoiding the Berlin by playing something else. Learn to play against it — the small edge is real.
stages.ready: You are comfortable in a queenless middlegame with a small structural plus.

progression.study: Fischer and Karpov for the classical treatment, Kasparov for the attacking version, Carlsen for the modern grind. Kramnik–Kasparov, London 2000 is the match that made the Berlin Wall famous.
progression.next: Add a second line against the Berlin, then start studying the Ruy's cousin structures — the Italian with d4 and the Scotch — so you can transpose when it suits you.

name: Scotch Game
tagline: Open the centre on move three. Far less theory than the Ruy, and it fights for an advantage immediately.

theory.big_idea: White plays d4 at once, exchanges in the centre and gets an open position with a small development lead. Where the Ruy Lopez builds pressure over thirty moves, the Scotch resolves the central tension immediately. The trade-off: releasing the tension gives Black clear equalising targets, so White's edge is small — but the positions are easy to understand and there is far less to memorise.
theory.structure: After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4, White has a pawn on e4 against Black's pawn on d6/d7 — a small space edge and a half-open d-file. In the Mieses main line, White ends up with a healthy 4v3 queenside majority while Black has doubled c-pawns and the bishop pair, exactly the sort of imbalance you can play for a win with.
white_plans: Occupy the centre with e4–e5 gaining space and driving Black's knight away.
Play against the doubled c-pawns with a healthy queenside majority; steer toward endgames.
Castle queenside in the Mieses line and push the kingside pawns with g3, Bg2, f4 and h4.
In the 4...Bc5 lines, kick the bishop with Nb3 or challenge it with Be3, and aim for a Maroczy-style bind with c4.
black_plans: 4...Bc5 hitting the knight on d4 and provoking a concession; then ...Qf6 and quick development.
4...Nf6 aiming for the Mieses lines with the bishop pair and pressure on White's e5-pawn.
Break with ...d5 as soon as possible to free the position — the standard antidote to a space advantage.
Target the e5-pawn with ...Qe7, ...Ba6 and ...O-O-O.
traps: 4.Nxd4 Qh4?! 5.Nc3! (not 5.Nf5?? Qxe4+) — Black's early queen sortie is bad but you must know the refutation.
In the Scotch Gambit (4.Bc4), 4...Bc5 5.Ng5?! Nh6! and White has nothing; do not chase f7 blindly.
4...Bc5 5.Nxc6 Qf6! is the point — Black regains the piece; White should meet 4...Bc5 with 5.Nb3 or 5.Be3.
theory.who: Play this if you want an open, principled 1.e4 opening without memorising a Ruy Lopez encyclopaedia. Kasparov revived it at world-championship level in the 1990s.

progression.arc: The Scotch is the fast route to a real 1.e4 repertoire: open positions, clear plans, and roughly a tenth of the Ruy Lopez's theory.

stages.goal: Know what to do after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 against each of Black's four replies.
learn: The two main branches: 4...Nf6 (Mieses) and 4...Bc5 (Classical). Learn one line against each and nothing more at first.
Why 5.Nxc6 is played in the Mieses — it damages Black's structure and buys the tempo for e4–e5.
The refutation of 4...Qh4: 5.Nc3! (never 5.Nf5?? Qxe4+).
stages.drill: Play the Scotch exclusively for two weeks. The positions repeat quickly and you will learn the patterns fast.
stages.mistake: Answering 4...Bc5 with 5.Nxc6? — Black plays 5...Qf6! and wins the piece back with a good game.
stages.ready: You can reach move eight in both main branches without hesitation.

stages.goal: Learn to play with and against doubled pawns and a space advantage.
learn: The Mieses structure: Black's doubled c-pawns against White's healthy queenside majority. That majority is your winning plan.
The double edge of the e5-pawn: it grabs space and it is a permanent target for ...Qe7, ...Ba6 and ...O-O-O.
When to castle queenside yourself and turn the game into a race.
stages.drill: Play out the Mieses tabiya after 9...O-O-O ten times from both sides. Notice how often the game is decided by whose attack lands first.
stages.mistake: Defending the e5-pawn passively. It is a spearhead, not a possession — sometimes you give it up for activity.
stages.ready: You can explain why the doubled c-pawns matter more in an endgame than a middlegame.

stages.goal: Convert the small opening edge into something.
learn: The queenside pawn majority: how to create a passed pawn against doubled pawns and trade into the endgame.
The kingside expansion with g3, Bg2, f4 and h4 in the opposite-castling lines.
Meeting ...d5 breaks: usually you take and blockade rather than push past.
stages.drill: Take five of your own Scotch games and mark the exact move where you stopped having a plan. That is your study list.
stages.mistake: Trading pieces without a reason. Your edge is space and structure — trade pawns to keep the structural plus, not pieces at random.
stages.ready: You have won a Scotch endgame purely on the queenside majority.

stages.goal: Add the gambit lines and the anti-Scotch systems.
learn: The Scotch Gambit 4.Bc4 as a second weapon, especially against opponents who prepare 4.Nxd4 lines.
The Göring Gambit 4.c3 for when you want the game to catch fire.
How Black avoids the Scotch entirely with 2...Nf6 (Petrov) or 2...d6 (Philidor) — you need a plan against both.
stages.drill: Prepare one complete line against the Petrov. It is the most common way strong players sidestep everything you have learned.
stages.mistake: Assuming Black must play 2...Nc6. At club level roughly one game in five will not.
stages.ready: Every Black second move has an answer in your file.

progression.study: Garry Kasparov's Scotch games from the early 1990s revived the whole opening. For the modern positional treatment, look at how Ian Nepomniachtchi and Anish Giri handle the Mieses.
progression.next: The Scotch pairs naturally with the Italian — same principles, different pace. Learn both and you can choose the character of the game on move three.

name: Four Knights Game
tagline: Both knights out before anything else. The most natural, most symmetrical open game there is.

theory.big_idea: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 all four knights are developed to their best squares and nothing is committed yet. The Four Knights is the purest expression of the opening principles: knights before bishops, fight for the centre, castle early. Because it is so symmetrical, the fight is about who breaks the symmetry first and on what terms — with 4.Bb5 (Spanish), 4.d4 (Scotch), 4.Bc4 (Italian), 4.g3 (Glek), or a gambit. It has a gentle reputation, but it is fully sound and still appears at the very top level.
theory.structure: Usually the classic Open Game skeleton: pawns on e4 and e5 with the d-pawns still home, all four knights developed. From there the structure depends entirely on White's fourth move. The Spanish keeps the tension and manoeuvres; the Scotch resolves the centre and gives White doubled c-pawns for Black in some lines; the Glek fianchettoes; and the gambits blow the centre open at once.
white_plans: The Spanish plan (4.Bb5): pin nothing, pressure e5, then the Metger structure with c3, d4 and slow manoeuvring — the same ideas as the Ruy Lopez but simpler.
The Scotch plan (4.d4): open the centre immediately and play against Black's doubled c-pawns with a small, clear edge.
The Glek plan (4.g3): fianchetto the bishop and treat the position like a reversed King's Indian, playing for d4 or f4 later.
The gambit plans (Belgrade 5.Nd5, Halloween 4.Nxe5): sacrifice a pawn or a piece for a huge lead in development and a big centre — surprise weapons that win a lot of club games.

The Ruy Lopez crossover: reach a Four Knights via the Morphy move order 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.Nc3 (the Tarrasch Variation), then use the Nd5 jump — a way to play the Four Knights with an extra Spanish flavour.
black_plans: Break the symmetry with the Rubinstein 4.Bb5 Nd4!, the most respected reply, which sidesteps all the slow manoeuvring.
The fork trick: against 4.Bc4, play 4...Nxe4! 5.Nxe4 d5 forking bishop and knight to reach an easy equal game.
Copy White's development, castle, and hit back in the centre with ...d5 at the right moment.
In the Metger, unpin with ...Bxc3, ...Qe7 and reroute the knight ...Nd8–e6 to kick the g5-bishop and support ...c5 or ...d5.
traps: Halloween Gambit shock: 4.Nxe5!? Nxe5 5.d4 forking two knights — Black is objectively winning a piece but must defend precisely, and many club players collapse under the central pawn roller.
The classic symmetry trap: after 4.Bb5 Bb4 5.O-O O-O 6.d3 d6, never copy blindly — 6...Bxc3 7.bxc3 and if Black keeps mirroring with 7...Ne7?! White gets a strong attack. Break the symmetry in time.
Belgrade Gambit greed: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nd5 Nxe4?! enters forced, only-move complications where one slip loses on the spot; the calm 5...Nxd5 or 5...Be7 is far safer.
Rubinstein point: 4.Bb5 Nd4 5.Bc4 Bc5 6.Nxe5? Qe7! and Black regains the piece with a better game — White should avoid grabbing e5.
theory.who: Play this if you want a sound, principled 1.e4 opening with far less theory than the Ruy Lopez, or if you want gambit surprise weapons (Belgrade, Halloween) that score heavily at club level. It is the perfect bridge from beginner openings to the classical main lines.

progression.arc: The Four Knights is the ideal first 'real' opening: it rewards the principles you already know, then quietly teaches you the manoeuvring ideas of the Ruy Lopez without the mountain of theory.

stages.goal: Reach the tabiya and pick your fourth move.
learn: The starting moves 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 — pure opening principles, played on autopilot.
Choose one fourth move to start with: 4.Bb5 (Spanish, classical) or 4.d4 (Scotch, low-theory and direct).
Why symmetry is dangerous for the copier: at some point Black must break it, and if White breaks it first with tempo, White is better.
stages.drill: Play twenty games committing to one fourth move. Notice how often opponents simply mirror you into trouble.
stages.mistake: Copying Black's moves back forever as White, or as Black copying White past the point where a concrete threat appears.
stages.ready: You reach the four-knights position without thinking and always have a plan for move four.

stages.goal: Understand the Metger structure and the doubled c-pawns.
learn: The Metger unpin: ...Bxc3, ...Qe7, ...Nd8–e6, and why the knight goes the long way round.
How doubled c-pawns are both a weakness (a target) and a strength (they support a big centre) — the central Four Knights bargain.
The two freeing breaks for Black: ...d5 (in the Scotch and Glek) and ...c5 (in the Spanish).
stages.drill: Play out the Metger main line to move twelve from both sides five times. Learn the knight route by hand.
stages.mistake: Trading on c6 too early as White — it repairs Black's structure and hands over the bishop pair for nothing.
stages.ready: You can explain what the doubled c-pawns do for and against you.

stages.goal: Play the middlegame the opening produces.
learn: The knight manoeuvre Nf3–d2–f1–e3–f5, the same slow build-up as the Ruy Lopez.
When to close the centre with d5 (play on the wings) versus keep the tension (piece play).
Meeting Black's ...Nd4 (Rubinstein) and the fork trick (against 4.Bc4) without getting worse.
stages.drill: Study ten Metger middlegames and mark where each side's knights ended up. Patterns will repeat.
stages.mistake: Drifting without a plan once development is done — the Four Knights punishes aimless play more than tactical openings do.
stages.ready: You have re-routed a knight to f5 or d5 and won a game from the resulting bind.

stages.goal: Add sharpness and cover the gambits from both sides.
learn: The Belgrade Gambit (5.Nd5) as an occasional surprise weapon, and the sound defences 5...Nxd5 and 5...Be7.
The Halloween Gambit (4.Nxe5) — how to attack with it, and, more importantly, how to refute it and keep the extra piece.
The Glek 4.g3 as a low-risk positional alternative when you want to avoid all the main-line theory.
stages.drill: Learn the Halloween Gambit refutation cold. You will be on the receiving end of it sooner or later.
stages.mistake: Entering the Belgrade's 5...Nxe4 complications unprepared — it is all forcing, only-move theory.
stages.ready: You are comfortable on both sides of at least one Four Knights gambit.

progression.study: For the classical Spanish Four Knights, study Savielly Tartakower and the old masters; for the modern positional Glek, look at Igor Glek's own games. Kasparov and Anand have both used the Scotch Four Knights at the top level.
progression.next: The Four Knights flows straight into the Ruy Lopez and the Scotch — the ideas transfer almost move for move. When you want more depth, those are the natural next steps.

name: Queen's Gambit
tagline: The most trusted 1.d4 opening in history. Not really a gambit at all.

theory.big_idea: White attacks Black's d5-pawn from the side with c4 instead of head-on. If Black takes with ...dxc4, the pawn cannot be held (b5 is always met by a4), and White simply recovers it while building a big centre with e4. If Black declines with ...e6 or ...c6, Black must accept a small structural or developmental concession. The whole opening is a fight over whether White gets to play e2–e4.
theory.structure: The defining structure is the Carlsbad: White pawns on a2, b2, c3, d4, e3 against Black pawns on a7, b7, c6, d5, f7. It arises from the Exchange Variation and it hands both sides a completely clear plan — White attacks on the queenside with a minority attack, Black attacks on the kingside with a piece storm. Learning the Carlsbad teaches you more about middlegame planning than any tactics book.
white_plans: The minority attack: push b2–b4–b5 to trade off on c6, leaving Black with a weak backward c-pawn on an open file.
Play for the e3–e4 break, converting the space advantage into an attack.
In the Accepted, regain the pawn with Bxc4 and build the ideal centre with e4, accepting an isolated d-pawn for activity.
Pile up on the c-file and infiltrate on c7/c8.
black_plans: Break with ...c5 (Tarrasch style) or ...e5, freeing the position at the cost of structure.
In the Carlsbad, attack on the kingside with ...Ne4, ...f5, ...Ng6 and a piece storm — Black is faster there because White's pawns are committed to the other wing.
Trade off pieces with the Tartakower plan (...b6, ...Bb7) to relieve the cramp.
The 'freeing manoeuvre' ...Nd7–f8–g6 or ...Nf6–e4 to trade a pair of pieces.
traps: The Elephant Trap: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nxd5?? Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+! 8.Qd2 Bxd2+ 9.Kxd2 Kxd8 and Black is a piece up.
Never try to defend the c4-pawn with 2...dxc4 3.e3 b5?? 4.a4 c6 5.axb5 cxb5 6.Qf3! forking a8 and b7.
The Rubinstein Trap: Black playing ...Nbd7 and then ...Re8 too early can drop a pawn to Nxd5!
theory.who: Play this if you want the most solid, most respected 1.d4 opening there is. Every world champion from Steinitz to Ding has played it.

progression.arc: The Queen's Gambit is the best strategic education in chess. Learn it and you will understand pawn structures for the rest of your life.

stages.goal: Know why the pawn cannot be held and get a healthy position against each defence.
learn: Why 2...dxc4 does not win a pawn: 3.e3 b5? 4.a4 c6 5.axb5 cxb5 6.Qf3! forks a8 and b7.
Your basic setup against the Declined: Nc3, Nf3, Bg5, e3, Bd3, Qc2, O-O. Same seven moves nearly every game.
The three main defences you will actually face: 2...e6 (Declined), 2...c6 (Slav), 2...dxc4 (Accepted).
stages.drill: Play twenty games with the Exchange Variation. One structure, one plan, endless repetition — this is the fastest way to improve at chess.
stages.mistake: Playing cxd5 at random. The Exchange is a commitment: you get a clear plan and Black gets the e-file and a free hand on the kingside.
stages.ready: You can set up the seven-move scheme against any Black move order.

stages.goal: Master the Carlsbad structure. It is the single most valuable structure in chess.
learn: The pawn skeleton: White a2-b2-c3-d4-e3 against Black a7-b7-c6-d5-f7. Learn to recognise it from any move order.
Why White plays on the queenside and Black on the kingside: your pawns point that way, and pawns decide where you attack.
The knight to e2 rather than f3 — it keeps the f-pawn free and allows Ng3 or Nf4.
stages.drill: Set up the Carlsbad and play only the minority attack: b4, a4, b5, bxc6. Do it ten times. Feel how the backward c-pawn appears.
stages.mistake: Starting the minority attack before your pieces are placed. Rab1 and Qc2 come first, then the pawns.
stages.ready: You can draw the Carlsbad structure from memory and name both sides' plans.

stages.goal: Learn the four plans available in the Carlsbad and how to choose between them.
learn: Plan A, the minority attack (b4–b5) — the workhorse.
Plan B, the central break e3–e4 — stronger when Black has committed to a kingside attack.
Plan C, the kingside pawn storm with f3 and g4 — for when Black's minor pieces have left that wing.
Plan D, piece pressure on the c-file with Rc1, Na4 and Nc5.
stages.drill: Take the position after 11.Rab1 and play each of the four plans once against an engine. Note which one it defends worst.
stages.mistake: Switching plans halfway. Each plan commits pawns, and pawns do not come back.
stages.ready: You choose your plan based on where Black's pieces are, not on habit.

stages.goal: Cover the whole 1.d4 d5 landscape and the resulting endgames.
learn: The Queen's Gambit Accepted, including the isolated-queen's-pawn positions that come with it.
The Slav and Semi-Slav — you will face them constantly, and the Meran and Botvinnik lines are theory-heavy.
Rook endgames with a queenside majority. Most Carlsbad games end there.
stages.drill: Study twenty of Botvinnik's or Karpov's Carlsbad games. Cover the moves and guess each one.
stages.mistake: Neglecting the Slav because the Declined is more common in books. In practice the Slav is everywhere.
stages.ready: You have a prepared answer to 2...e6, 2...c6, 2...dxc4 and 2...Nf6.

progression.study: Capablanca and Botvinnik for the classical minority attack, Karpov for the modern squeeze, Kramnik and Ding Liren for the current treatment.
progression.next: Add the Catalan. It uses the same c4/d4 pawns with a different bishop and gives you a second, quieter way to play for a win.

name: London System
tagline: One setup against almost anything. The lowest-theory way to play 1.d4 well.

theory.big_idea: White plays the same first five or six moves regardless of what Black does: d4, Bf4, e3, Nf3, c3, Bd3 (and often Nbd2, h3, O-O). The bishop gets outside the pawn chain before e3 locks it in — this is the single most important move-order point in the whole system. The result is a solid, flexible position with no weaknesses, from which White plays either Ne5 with a kingside attack or a slow queenside expansion.
theory.structure: White pawns on d4, e3, c3 form a small pyramid — extremely hard to attack. The dark-squared bishop sits outside on f4 or g3 controlling the b8–h2 diagonal. The signature attacking pattern is Ne5, f4, Qf3–h3 and Rf3–h3, throwing pieces at h7.
white_plans: Plant a knight on e5, support it with f4 and Nd2–f3, then swing the queen and rook to the h-file.
Trade dark-squared bishops on d6, then use the resulting dark-square control and pressure on c7/e5.
Queenside expansion with b4, a4 and Nb3–c5, especially when Black castles kingside and plays ...c5.
The 'Barry/Jobava' aggressive version: Nc3 and e4 for a fast central break.
black_plans: Hit d4 immediately with ...c5 and ...Qb6 pressuring b2 — the sharpest test of the system.
Play ...Bd6 to trade off White's good bishop, then ...Qxd6 and ...e5.
Set up a King's Indian structure with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6, ...Nbd7 and break with ...e5.
Develop the c8-bishop early with ...Bf5 before ...e6 — the mirror image of White's own idea.
traps: If White plays e3 before Bf4, the bishop is stuck behind the pawn chain — this is the mistake that turns a good London into a bad one.
After ...Qb6 hitting b2, White should not panic: Qb3, Nc3 (offering the pawn) or Qc1 all hold. Grabbing with ...Qxb2 often costs Black the queen after Nb5 and Rb1 ideas.
Watch out for ...Nh5 hitting the f4-bishop. Standard answers: Bg3 or Be5, or pre-empt with h3 and Bh2.
theory.who: Play this if you want to spend your study time on middlegames and endgames instead of opening theory. It is genuinely sound — Carlsen, Kamsky and Gukesh all use it.

progression.arc: The London gets you a good position with almost no memorisation. The catch is that the middlegames are entirely up to you.

stages.goal: Learn the setup and, above all, the move order.
learn: The setup: d4, Bf4, e3, Nf3, c3, Bd3, Nbd2, h3, O-O. Nine moves, playable against almost anything.
The one rule that matters: Bf4 before e3. Every bad London starts by locking the bishop in.
Why the knight goes to d2 and not c3 — the c-pawn must stay on c3 supporting d4.
stages.drill: Play the nine-move setup in fifty blitz games. It should take you under a minute total.
stages.mistake: Playing on autopilot into a bad version. If Black plays an early ...c5 and ...Qb6, you must respond, not continue the routine.
stages.ready: You can reach the full setup against 1...d5, 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 without thinking.

stages.goal: Recognise which of three middlegames you have landed in.
learn: Type 1 — Black plays ...e6 and ...Bd6: you decline the bishop trade with Bg3, play Ne5 and attack the kingside.
Type 2 — Black fianchettoes: you switch plans entirely, play c4 and treat it as a Queen's Gambit.
Type 3 — Black plays ...c5 and ...Qb6 hitting b2: you need a concrete answer (Qb3, Qc1 or the Nc3 pawn offer).
stages.drill: Write down your answer to ...Qb6 and memorise it. It is the only real theory the London requires.
stages.mistake: Panicking when b2 is attacked and playing Qc1 passively every time. Sometimes offering the pawn is much stronger.
stages.ready: You can name which of the three types you are in by move six.

stages.goal: Turn the solid position into an attack.
learn: The attacking machine: Ne5, f4, Qf3–h3, Rf3–h3 and the Bxh6 sacrifice when Black weakens with ...h6.
The trade-on-d6 plan: swap dark-squared bishops, then use the dark squares and the c-file.
The queenside plan: b4, a4, Nb3–c5 when Black castles kingside and commits to ...c5.
stages.drill: Study the Bxh7+ and Bxh6 sacrifice patterns until you can calculate them in ten seconds. The London produces them constantly.
stages.mistake: Playing solidly forever. The London is not a draw machine — if you never attack, strong opponents simply equalise and outplay you.
stages.ready: You have won a game with the Qf3–h3 build-up.

stages.goal: Add sharpness and cover the anti-London systems.
learn: The Jobava London (2.Nc3 and 3.Bf4) for a much sharper version with e4 ideas.
The lines where Black plays an early ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, mirroring your own idea.
Endgames with the c3–d4–e3 structure: they are drawish unless you create an outside passer, so learn to create one.
stages.drill: Play the Jobava version for a month and compare your results. Many players find it suits them better.
stages.mistake: Believing the London is 'safe'. It is sound, which is different — the safety has to come from your play.
stages.ready: You have two versions of the system and choose between them by opponent.

progression.study: Gata Kamsky brought the London back to elite level; Magnus Carlsen and Gukesh Dommaraju both use it as a serious weapon. For attacking models, look at Baadur Jobava's games.
progression.next: When you want more, learn the Queen's Gambit properly. The London will still be there as a low-preparation option for fast time controls.

name: Catalan Opening
tagline: d4 and c4 plus a fianchettoed bishop. Positional pressure that lasts into the endgame.

theory.big_idea: White combines the Queen's Gambit pawns (d4, c4) with a king's-Indian style fianchetto (g3, Bg2). The bishop on g2 — the 'Catalan bishop' — fires down the long diagonal at b7, d5 and c6 and it never stops. White is often willing to give up the c4-pawn for a while, because the resulting pressure and the eventual recovery of the pawn is worth more than the material. Games are decided in the endgame, when the Catalan bishop is still the best piece on the board.
theory.structure: White pawns on d4 and (temporarily) c4, with the fianchetto on g3. Black usually plays ...d5 and ...e6. The critical structural question is whether Black takes on c4 (Open Catalan, sharp) or holds with ...c6/...Nbd7 (Closed Catalan, cramped but solid).
white_plans: Regain the c4-pawn with Qa4/Qc2 and Ne5, keeping the bishop's diagonal open.
Push e2–e4 to gain the full centre once Black's pieces are tied down.
Play a4 to stop ...b5, then invade on c6 or the c-file.
Trade queens and grind: the Catalan bishop is at its most powerful in endgames.
black_plans: Take on c4 and try to hold with ...a6 and ...b5, gaining queenside space.
Block the diagonal with ...c6 and ...b5, or neutralise it directly with ...Bb7 and ...Be4.
The freeing break ...c5 or ...e5, the standard antidotes to a space disadvantage.
Play ...Bb4+ early to provoke Bd2 and gain time for ...dxc4 and ...a6/...b5.
traps: Trying to hold the pawn with ...b5 and ...c6 often collapses to a well-timed a4 or Ne5 hitting c6 and b5 at once.
Black's ...Bb4+ lines must be met with Bd2 (not Nc3, which blocks the bishop's support of the c-pawn recovery).
Never let the g2-bishop get shut in permanently — if Black plays ...c6 and ...b5, look for e4 or a4 immediately.
theory.who: Play this if you enjoy positions where you have no risk of losing and endless small chances to win. Kramnik, Anand, Ding and Carlsen have all used it as a main weapon.

progression.arc: The Catalan is a long game. You accept a tiny edge on move ten and you are still pressing on move sixty. It rewards patience more than any other opening.

stages.goal: Get the setup right and know how to recover the c4-pawn.
learn: The setup: d4, c4, g3, Bg2, Nf3, O-O. The order matters mostly for avoiding the Nimzo-Indian.
The two pawn-recovery methods after ...dxc4: Qa4+/Qc2–xc4, and Ne5 hitting c6 and c4 at once.
Why Bd2 rather than Nc3 against ...Bb4+ — the knight would block your own c-file pressure.
stages.drill: Play ten games where Black takes on c4 and hold yourself to recovering it within six moves.
stages.mistake: Chasing the pawn immediately with a4 and Na3. Development and the bishop's diagonal are worth more than the pawn for several moves.
stages.ready: You are comfortable being a pawn down for five or six moves.

stages.goal: Understand what the g2-bishop is actually doing.
learn: The long diagonal a8–h1 and the three squares that matter on it: d5, c6, b7.
Open Catalan (Black takes on c4) versus Closed (Black holds with ...c6) — completely different games.
Why ...c6 is annoying: it blocks the diagonal with a pawn, so your answer is the e4 break.
stages.drill: Set up the Closed Catalan and play only for the e4 break. Ten games. Notice how much better your position is once it lands.
stages.mistake: Letting the g2-bishop stay blocked. If you cannot play e4 or a4, you have no advantage at all.
stages.ready: You can look at a Catalan and say in one sentence what your bishop is doing.

stages.goal: Learn the squeeze.
learn: a4 against the b5-pawn — undermining the base of Black's queenside chain is the standard method.
Ne5 and Nd2–c4 or Nd2–b3, piling onto c5, c6 and a5.
The queen trade. The Catalan bishop is stronger in the endgame than the middlegame — trading queens is often an improvement.
stages.drill: Take twenty Catalan games by Kramnik and note the move on which he trades queens. It is almost never a concession.
stages.mistake: Looking for a kingside attack. The Catalan wins on the queenside and in the endgame.
stages.ready: You have converted a Catalan endgame where your only advantage was the bishop.

stages.goal: Handle everything Black tries to avoid it.
learn: The ...c5 lines that steer into a fianchetto Benoni — a different but equally good game for White.
The Bogo-Indian (...Bb4+) and Queen's Indian (...b6) move orders.
Open Catalan theory with ...a6 and ...b5 — this is the main line and it is genuinely deep.
stages.drill: Prepare a line against 3...c5 and 3...Bb4+ before you play the Catalan in a serious game.
stages.mistake: Playing g3 too early and allowing a favourable Nimzo-Indian move order. Know why you chose 3.g3 over 3.Nf3.
stages.ready: Every Black third move has a prepared answer.

progression.study: Vladimir Kramnik made the Catalan a world-championship weapon; Ding Liren, Anish Giri and Fabiano Caruana all use it as a main line today.
progression.next: Pair it with the Queen's Gambit Exchange. Between them you can steer almost any 1.d4 game into a structure you understand better than your opponent.

name: Sicilian Defence
tagline: The most popular and most successful answer to 1.e4. Black plays to win, not to equalise.

theory.big_idea: 1...c5 refuses symmetry from move one. Black trades a flank pawn (c) for a central pawn (d) and gets, in return: a half-open c-file pointing straight at c2 and White's king if it castles queenside, and a 2-to-1 central pawn majority. The cost is that White gets a lead in development and space, and usually gets to attack first. Every Sicilian is a race — White attacks the kingside, Black attacks the queenside, and whoever is faster wins.
theory.structure: After ...cxd4 the defining structure is the 'Sicilian small centre': Black pawns on d6 and e6/e5 against White's e4. The half-open c-file is Black's motorway. In the Najdorf and Dragon, White typically castles long and storms the kingside with f3, g4, h4; Black storms the queenside with ...b5, ...b4, ...a5 and sacrifices on c3.
white_plans: English Attack: Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O, then g4 and h4 with a direct pawn storm.
Yugoslav Attack against the Dragon: Bc4, Bе3, Qd2, O-O-O, h4–h5 and Bh6 trading the fianchetto bishop.
The positional bind: c4 and Be2 (Maroczy Bind), taking away ...b5 and ...d5 and squeezing Black to death.
The classical setup with Be2, O-O, f4 and a central e5 break.
black_plans: Queenside expansion with ...a6, ...b5, ...b4 hitting the c3-knight, plus ...Rc8 and the exchange sacrifice ...Rxc3!
Fight for the d5 square — the whole Najdorf is about whether Black gets in ...d5 in one move.
The Dragon bishop on g7 pointing down the long diagonal at b2 and White's queenside king.
Trade off White's dangerous attackers with ...Nxd4 or ...Ne5–c4.
traps: Beware the Siberian Trap in the Smith-Morra: after ...Qc7 and ...Nf6, if White plays Nd5?? then ...Nxe4! wins.
In the Najdorf Poisoned Pawn (6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6 8.Qd2 Qxb2), Black's queen goes on a raid — this is one of the most analysed positions in chess. Do not enter it unprepared.
Black must never delay too long: many Sicilians are lost to a quick Nd5 or Nf5 sacrifice ripping open the centre before Black castles.
theory.who: Play this if you want winning chances with Black and you do not mind sharp, theory-heavy positions. Fischer, Kasparov, Anand and Carlsen all built careers on it.

progression.arc: The Sicilian is the biggest body of theory in chess. The way through it is to learn one variation properly rather than six badly.

stages.goal: Choose one Sicilian and understand the trade you are making.
learn: The core bargain: you give up a wing pawn for a centre pawn and receive the half-open c-file. Everything else follows from that.
Pick one: Najdorf (sharpest, most theory), Accelerated Dragon (solid, less theory), Sveshnikov (unbalanced, forcing), Kan/Taimanov (flexible, low theory).
The Anti-Sicilians you will actually face more than the Open: 2.Nc3, 2.c3 (Alapin), 3.Bb5 (Rossolimo/Moscow) and the Smith-Morra.
stages.drill: Prepare your Anti-Sicilian answers first. Below master level you will meet 2.c3 and 3.Bb5 more often than the Open Sicilian.
stages.mistake: Learning twenty moves of the Najdorf and nothing against 2.c3. You will lose to the Alapin repeatedly and never reach your preparation.
stages.ready: You have one line against every White second and third move, written down.

stages.goal: Learn your chosen structure's skeleton and the squares that decide it.
learn: In the Najdorf: the d5 square. Every move in the opening is about whether Black achieves ...d5 in one move or not.
In the Dragon and Accelerated Dragon: the long diagonal and the g7-bishop. It is worth more than a rook in many positions.
In every Sicilian: the half-open c-file, the exchange sacrifice ...Rxc3, and the ...b5–b4 lever.
stages.drill: Play out your tabiya twenty times from move ten. Do not study new lines until the tabiya is second nature.
stages.mistake: Playing ...d5 because it is 'freeing' when it loses a pawn or a piece. Count the defenders every time.
stages.ready: You know the key square in your variation and can explain what happens if you never control it.

stages.goal: Win the race.
learn: The counting principle in opposite-castling positions: count how many moves each attack needs. That number, not the evaluation, decides the game.
The standard sacrifices: ...Rxc3 (exchange), ...Nxe4 (opening lines), ...b4 and ...a5–a4 (pure pawns).
When to defend instead: ...h5 stopping the g-pawn, ...Kb8 and ...Rc8 tucking away.
stages.drill: Take ten opposite-castling Sicilians and, at move fifteen, count both attacks before looking at the result. Train the counting.
stages.mistake: Defending passively. In a race, one defensive move is one attacking move you did not make — defend only when the arithmetic demands it.
stages.ready: You can look at an English Attack position and say who is faster, with a reason.

stages.goal: Depth in your line, plus the endgames.
learn: Your variation's deepest branches — in the Najdorf that means the Poisoned Pawn and the 6.Bg5 complex.
The Maroczy Bind and how to break it: ...b5 sacrifices, ...Nxd4 trades and the ...f5 break.
Sicilian endgames: the queenside majority Black often has, and why a good knight beats a bad bishop in these structures.
stages.drill: Analyse five of your own losses in the Sicilian and classify them: lost the race, lost the structure, or lost to preparation. Fix the biggest category.
stages.mistake: Switching variations after a loss. Depth beats breadth in the Sicilian by an enormous margin.
stages.ready: You have a line you have played fifty times and still find new ideas in.

progression.study: Fischer and Kasparov for the Najdorf, Carlsen and Caruana for the modern Sveshnikov — their 2018 World Championship match is the best available course in it.
progression.next: Once one Sicilian is deep, add a second as a surprise weapon rather than starting over. The structures overlap more than the move orders suggest.

name: French Defence
tagline: A pawn chain, a bad bishop, and a devastating counterattack. Black chooses structure over freedom.

theory.big_idea: 1...e6 prepares ...d5 with pawn support. Black accepts one real problem — the c8-bishop is locked behind the e6-pawn — in exchange for a rock-solid pawn chain and a very clear plan: attack the base of White's chain with ...c5 and ...f6. The French is the most 'plan-driven' opening in chess. You know from move three exactly what you are doing for the next twenty-five moves.
theory.structure: The classic French chain: White pawns d4–e5, Black pawns d5–e6. A pawn chain is attacked at its base, so Black plays ...c5 (hitting d4) and later ...f6 (hitting e5). White defends with c3 and f4 and tries to exploit the extra kingside space. Almost every French middlegame is about these two breaks.
white_plans: Advance Variation (3.e5): grab space, defend d4 with c3 and Nf3, then attack on the kingside with Bd3, Ne2, h4 and Nf4.
Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5): accept doubled c-pawns for the bishop pair and a huge attack with Qg4 hitting g7.
Tarrasch (3.Nd2): avoid the pin, keep the structure clean and play for an isolated-queen's-pawn edge.
Exchange (3.exd5): a solid, symmetrical, drawish structure.
black_plans: Hit the base of the chain with ...c5, then ...Qb6 and ...Nc6 piling on d4.
Undermine the front of the chain with ...f6 once the queenside is secure.
Solve the bad bishop: ...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7–b5, or ...Bd7–e8–h5.
In the Winawer, target White's doubled c-pawns and the dark squares with ...Qa5 and ...Ba6.
traps: In the Winawer Poisoned Pawn (6...Ne7 7.Qg4 Qc7 8.Qxg7 Rg8 9.Qxh7 cxd4), Black gives up two kingside pawns for a huge lead in development — one of the sharpest lines in all of chess.
Never play ...cxd4 too early in the Advance; keeping the tension is Black's main source of pressure.
The Milner-Barry Gambit (Advance, 6.Bd3 cxd4 7.cxd4 Bd7 8.O-O Nxd4 9.Nxd4 Qxd4 10.Nc3!) — Black must know how to defend the resulting attack.
theory.who: Play this if you like clear structural plans, you do not mind a cramped position, and you want to punish White for over-extending. The French wins more games by counterattack than any other defence.

progression.arc: The French teaches you pawn chains better than any other opening, and pawn chains are the skeleton of positional chess.

stages.goal: Accept the bad bishop and learn the one universal plan.
learn: The plan in every French: hit the base of White's chain with ...c5, then the front with ...f6. That is the whole opening.
The four things White can do on move three: 3.e5 (Advance), 3.Nc3 (Classical/Winawer), 3.Nd2 (Tarrasch), 3.exd5 (Exchange).
Why ...Qb6 is the key move in the Advance — it hits d4 a third time and b2 at the same time.
stages.drill: Play the Advance from the Black side twenty times, aiming only for ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and pressure on d4.
stages.mistake: Trading on d4 too early. The tension on d4 is your entire source of pressure; releasing it hands White a free hand.
stages.ready: You can explain, without a board, why ...c5 comes before ...Nf6.

stages.goal: Solve the light-squared bishop, permanently.
learn: Route 1: ...b6 and ...Ba6, trading it for White's good bishop.
Route 2: ...Bd7–b5 or ...Bd7–a4, using the queenside.
Route 3: ...Bd7–e8–h5, the slow route to the kingside.
Route 4: leave it and play with pieces on the dark squares instead — sometimes correct.
stages.drill: In your next ten French games, write down on move ten which route you have chosen. If you cannot name one, that is the problem.
stages.mistake: Playing ...Nf6 and ...Be7 and hoping the bishop sorts itself out. It never does.
stages.ready: You choose the bishop's route by move ten, deliberately.

stages.goal: Counterattack rather than defend.
learn: The ...f6 break: when it opens the f-file for you and when it just weakens e6.
Queenside play with ...a5, ...Rc8, ...Na5–c4 and the pressure on c3 or c2.
Meeting White's kingside attack: ...h6 and ...g6 are usually wrong; counterattack in the centre instead.
stages.drill: Study ten games where Black wins with ...f6 and ten where ...f6 backfires. Write down the difference.
stages.mistake: Sitting still. The French is cramped, and a cramped position that never breaks out simply loses slowly.
stages.ready: You have won a game where White attacked the kingside and you won on the other wing.

stages.goal: Handle the sharp lines and the endgames.
learn: The Winawer with its doubled c-pawns and the Poisoned Pawn — Black's most ambitious try.
The Tarrasch and the isolated-pawn positions it produces; you need to know both sides of an IQP.
French endgames: the bad bishop is a real long-term problem, so learn which trades help you.
stages.drill: Learn the Winawer Poisoned Pawn to move fifteen from both sides, even if you never play it. The patterns appear everywhere.
stages.mistake: Fearing the Exchange Variation. It looks drawish; play ...Nf6, ...Bd6, ...O-O and ...c6 and play for a win with the extra tempo pattern.
stages.ready: You are comfortable against all four of White's third moves.

progression.study: Mikhail Botvinnik and Viktor Korchnoi built the modern French. For sharp modern play, look at Alexander Morozevich and Wesley So.
progression.next: The French and Caro-Kann share almost every idea. Learning the Caro-Kann second is fast and gives you a second answer to 1.e4.

name: Caro-Kann Defence
tagline: Everything the French does, but without the bad bishop. The most structurally sound reply to 1.e4.

theory.big_idea: 1...c6 prepares ...d5 with pawn support, exactly like the French — but with a crucial difference: the c8-bishop gets out to f5 or g4 before the ...e6 pawn locks it in. Black gets a French position with the French's main problem already solved. The price is a tempo (the c-pawn takes two moves to reach c5) and a slightly passive position. The Caro-Kann is the choice of players who want to reach a good endgame with a healthy structure.
theory.structure: After the Classical (3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4), Black has pawns on c6, e6 and a solid, symmetrical, weakness-free structure. Black is slightly cramped but has literally nothing to attack. In the Advance Variation the position becomes French-like but with the bishop already outside. In the Panov-Botvinnik, White gets an isolated queen's pawn and a sharp attacking game.
white_plans: Classical (3.Nc3): trade on e4, chase the bishop with h4–h5, castle queenside and attack.
Advance (3.e5): grab space and harass the f5-bishop with Nf3, Be2 and h4/Nh4.
Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4): open the game, take an isolated d-pawn and play for a kingside attack.
Exchange (3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3): quiet, symmetrical, with a slow minority attack.
black_plans: Develop the light-squared bishop outside the chain first, then play ...e6 — the whole point of the opening.
Trade off pieces and head for an endgame where the healthy structure counts.
Break with ...c5 (in the Advance) or ...e5 (in the Classical) once development is complete.
Meet a kingside attack by castling queenside or leaving the king in the centre in closed positions.
traps: Never play 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5.Qe2 Ngf6?? 6.Nd6# — the smothered mate every Caro-Kann player must know.
In the Advance, ...Bf5 4.h4!? h5 5.Bd3 is a genuine try — Black must know to take with ...Bxd3.
After 4...Bf5 5.Ng3 Bg6 6.h4 h6 7.Nf3, do not forget 7...e6! — 7...Nf6? 8.Ne5 is very unpleasant.
theory.who: Play this if you want a solid, low-risk defence to 1.e4 that still gives real winning chances in the endgame. Karpov, Anand and Carlsen have all used it as a main weapon.

stages.goal: Learn the one rule that defines the whole opening.
learn: The rule: develop the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6. Break it and you have a worse French.
White's four options: 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 (Classical), 3.e5 (Advance), 3.exd5 (Exchange/Panov), 2.c4 (Accelerated Panov).
The mate you must know: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5.Qe2 Ngf6?? 6.Nd6#.
stages.drill: Play the Classical twenty times, focusing only on getting ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6 in the right order.
stages.mistake: Playing ...Bf5 when White can hit it with Qb3 or Nh4 favourably. Check the tactics before every bishop move.
stages.ready: You never lock the bishop in behind ...e6.

stages.goal: Learn to be slightly worse and completely safe.
learn: In the Classical, Black has no weaknesses at all — the plan is to trade pieces and reach an equal endgame.
In the Advance, the plan is the same as the French: ...c5 at the base of the chain, but with your bishop already out.

name: King's Indian Defence
tagline: Give White the whole centre, then blow up the kingside. The most aggressive answer to 1.d4.

theory.big_idea: Black deliberately allows White to build a huge pawn centre with c4, d4 and e4, then attacks it from a distance with a fianchettoed bishop and the break ...e5. When White closes the centre with d4–d5, the position becomes locked and both sides attack on opposite wings: White pushes c4–c5 on the queenside, Black pushes ...f5–f4 and ...g5–g4 at White's king. It is the purest attacking race in chess, and the side that is one tempo faster usually wins by force.
theory.structure: The defining structure is the Mar del Plata: locked pawns on c4/d5/e4 for White against c7/d6/e5 for Black. This diagonal pawn wall determines everything — White's pawns point at the queenside, so White attacks there; Black's point at the kingside, so Black attacks there. Neither side defends. Whoever arrives first wins.
white_plans: Close the centre with d5, then break with c5 and pile onto the c-file and c7.
Play the Sämisch with f3, Be3 and O-O-O, and storm the kingside instead — turning Black's own plan against them.
The Fianchetto Variation with g3: a calm, safe way to blunt the Bg7 and steer the game toward a positional Benoni.
Trade off the g7-bishop with Be3–h6 or Bg5 and Qd2 — Black's attack dies without it.
black_plans: Break with ...e5, then re-route the knights (...Ne7 or ...Nd7) out of the way of the f-pawn.
The pawn storm: ...f5, ...f4, ...g5, ...g4, ...h5 and often a rook lift ...Rf6–h6.
Sacrifice material to open the h-file or the g-file. In many KID games Black is a piece down and completely winning.
Meet a queenside break with ...a5 and ...Nc5, blocking the c-file with a knight.
traps: Do not play ...e5 too early against 4.e4 — check that White cannot answer dxe5 favourably.
In the Mar del Plata, if Black plays ...f5 before securing the knight route, White can hit with exf5 gxf5 and Ng5 or f4 with a strong attack.
The Bayonet Attack (9.b4) is White's most testing modern try — Black must know 9...Nh5 or 9...a5.
theory.who: Play this if you want to attack from move one with the black pieces and you accept that you will be objectively worse for the first thirty moves. Fischer, Kasparov and Radjabov made it famous.

progression.arc: The King's Indian is a bet: you will be objectively worse for thirty moves and then checkmate someone. Learn to enjoy that.

stages.goal: Learn the six-move setup and the one break that matters.

name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
tagline: Pin the knight, trade it off, and play against the doubled pawns. The most respected defence to 1.d4.

theory.big_idea: 3...Bb4 pins the c3-knight, which is the piece guarding e4. Black is not fighting for the centre with pawns — Black is fighting for one square, e4, with pieces. Usually Black trades the bishop for the knight, giving White the bishop pair but leaving White with doubled c-pawns. The rest of the game is a clean philosophical argument: White's two bishops and open lines against Black's superior structure and control of the light squares.
theory.structure: The archetype is the Sämisch structure: White pawns on c3, c4, d4 (doubled c-pawns) against Black's a7, b7, c5, d6, e6. If the position opens, White's bishops dominate. If it stays closed, the doubled c-pawns are simply weak. Black therefore blockades with ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6 and ...Na5, and White strives to play e3–e4 and open lines.
white_plans: Rubinstein (4.e3): quiet development, then Bd3, Nf3, O-O and a central break with e4 or dxc5.
Classical (4.Qc2): pre-empt the doubled pawns by recapturing on c3 with the queen. White gets the bishop pair with no structural damage — at the cost of two tempi.
Sämisch (4.a3): force the trade immediately, accept the doubled pawns and go all-in on e3–e4 and a kingside attack.
Build the big centre with f3 and e4 and use the bishop pair in an open position.
black_plans: Trade on c3, then blockade the doubled pawns with ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6 and ...Na5 hitting c4.
Keep the bishop and play ...d5 and ...c5, treating it like a Queen's Gambit with an extra active bishop.
Control e4 with ...Ne4, ...b6, ...Bb7 and ...f5 — the Nimzowitsch dream setup.
Trade off White's bishop pair advantage at every opportunity.
traps: In the 4.Qc2 lines, do not automatically trade on c3 — White recaptures with the queen and there are no doubled pawns.
Watch for the Qd1–a4+ trick winning the loose bishop on b4 if Black plays ...c5 too early.
After 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd3 d5 6.Nf3 c5, Black must know 7.O-O dxc4 8.Bxc4 and the resulting isolated-pawn structures.
theory.who: Play this if you want a defence that is theoretically sound at every level and rewards positional understanding. It is arguably the single best answer to 1.d4 ever devised.

progression.arc: The Nimzo-Indian is the most respected defence to 1.d4 because it asks a question that has no clean answer. It rewards understanding over memory.

stages.goal: Understand why 3...Bb4 is a good move at all.
learn: The pin on c3 stops e4. Black is not fighting for the centre with pawns but preventing White from occupying it.
White's four main replies: 4.e3 (Rubinstein), 4.Qc2 (Classical), 4.a3 (Sämisch), 4.f3 and 4.Nf3.
The move-order problem: after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6, White can play 3.Nf3 and you never get the Nimzo. Pick a second defence now.
stages.drill: Prepare your answer to 3.Nf3 before your first Nimzo game — Queen's Indian (...b6), Bogo-Indian (...Bb4+) or Ragozin (...d5).
stages.mistake: Trading on c3 automatically. Against 4.Qc2 White recaptures with the queen and there are no doubled pawns to attack.
stages.ready: You have a complete answer to 3.Nf3 as well as to 3.Nc3.

stages.goal: Learn to play against doubled pawns — and to know when they are not weak.
learn: The Sämisch structure: White c3, c4, d4 against your c5, d6, e6. Blockade with ...Na5 and ...Ba6 and the c4-pawn falls.
The rule that decides everything: doubled pawns are weak in a closed position and strong in an open one, because they support a big centre.
Your job after trading on c3: keep the position closed and trade pieces, never open lines for the bishops.
stages.drill: Play ten Sämisch positions with the plan ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6, ...Na5 and nothing else. See how often c4 simply drops.
stages.mistake: Opening the centre after giving up the bishop pair. Every open file you create is a gift to White's two bishops.
stages.ready: You can look at a doubled-pawn position and say whether they are a weakness or a strength.

stages.goal: Master the three middlegame types the Nimzo produces.
learn: Type 1 — the isolated queen's pawn (from 4.e3 lines): blockade d5, trade minor pieces, win the endgame.
Type 2 — hanging pawns on c4 and d4: attack them with ...Rc8 and ...Na5 and force one to advance.
Type 3 — the blockade against doubled pawns: knight to c5, bishop to a6, and total control of the light squares.
stages.drill: Take five of your Nimzo games and classify each middlegame into one of the three types. If you cannot, that is the study you need.
stages.mistake: Playing all three types the same way. The plan comes from the structure, and the Nimzo produces three different ones.
stages.ready: You name the structure type before you choose a move.

stages.goal: Depth in your chosen branch plus the endgames.
learn: One deep line against 4.Qc2 — currently the critical test at every level.
The Ragozin and Vienna transpositions, which arise constantly from Nimzo move orders.
Bishop-versus-knight endgames. The Nimzo is a machine for producing them and they decide half your games.
stages.drill: Study twenty Karpov or Kramnik games in the Nimzo, guessing every Black move. It is the best positional training available.
stages.mistake: Neglecting endgame study. The Nimzo produces small, technical advantages — you need the technique to convert them.
stages.ready: You can convert a one-pawn or good-knight-versus-bad-bishop endgame reliably.

progression.study: Aron Nimzowitsch invented it, Capablanca and Karpov perfected the positional treatment, and Kramnik and Caruana carry it today.
progression.next: Pair it with the Queen's Indian or Ragozin so that 3.Nf3 does not take you out of preparation. Together they form a complete 1.d4 defence.

name: Slav Defence
tagline: Support d5 with the c-pawn and keep the good bishop. The Caro-Kann of 1.d4.

theory.big_idea: Against the Queen's Gambit, Black must support d5. The Queen's Gambit Declined does it with ...e6, which locks the c8-bishop in. The Slav does it with ...c6, keeping the bishop's path to f5 and g4 open. Black's basic plan is to develop the bishop outside, then play ...e6 and ...dxc4 at a moment when the pawn can be held with ...b5 — grabbing genuine queenside space. It is the soundest, least compromising answer to 1.d4 there is.
theory.structure: Black keeps pawns on c6 and d5 with a healthy, unbreakable structure. In the main line Black takes on c4 and holds with ...b5, ...a6 and ...Bb7, gaining queenside space. In the Semi-Slav (with ...e6 too) the c8-bishop is temporarily locked in but Black gets the powerful ...c5 and ...e5 breaks. In the Exchange Slav the position is completely symmetrical and famously drawish.
white_plans: Play a4 early to stop ...b5 and take the b5 square for a knight or bishop.
Build the centre with e3, Bxc4 and e4, converting into a big pawn centre.
In the Exchange Slav, play the minority attack with b4–b5 on the queenside.
In the Semi-Slav, launch the Botvinnik or Anti-Moscow gambits with e4 and g4 — some of the sharpest theory in chess.
black_plans: Develop the bishop to f5 or g4 before playing ...e6 — the single defining idea of the whole opening.
Take on c4 and hold with ...b5, gaining queenside space and a queenside pawn majority.
The Meran plan: ...dxc4, ...b5, ...a6 and the central break ...c5.
Trade into a good endgame with the healthy structure and queenside majority.
traps: Do not play ...Bf5 before ...dxc4 in some move orders — White can hit with Qb3 forking b7 and d5.
After 4...dxc4 5.a4, remember that ...b5?? 6.axb5 cxb5 7.b3! wins the pawn back with a great position.
In the Semi-Slav Botvinnik (5.Bg5 dxc4 6.e4 b5 7.e5 h6 8.Bh4 g5), do not enter without preparation — it is one of the most forcing lines in existence.
theory.who: Play this if you want a defence to 1.d4 that is completely sound, gives you a healthy structure, and does not require you to accept a bad bishop or a cramped position.

progression.arc: The Slav is the defence you can play for thirty years without ever having a structurally bad position. The depth is in the details.

stages.goal: Understand why ...c6 beats ...e6 for supporting d5.
learn: The whole point: ...c6 supports d5 without locking in the c8-bishop. Get the bishop out before you play ...e6.
The main line move order: 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 dxc4 5.a4 Bf5. Know why a4 is forced and what it weakens.
The three families: Main Line Slav, Semi-Slav (with ...e6) and Exchange Slav.
stages.drill: Play the main line twenty times and note that b4 is available to you every game because White played a4.
stages.mistake: Taking on c4 before ...c6 is in. Without the c-pawn ready to support ...b5, the capture just loses a tempo.
stages.ready: You never play ...e6 before the bishop is developed, unless you have chosen the Semi-Slav deliberately.

stages.goal: Learn the queenside majority and what it is worth.
learn: After ...dxc4 and ...b5, you own a queenside pawn majority. That is a long-term endgame asset.
The b4 square that White's a4 permanently weakens — your bishop and knight both want it.
The Exchange Slav's symmetry: the whole game is about the c-file and one tempo.
stages.drill: Play ten Exchange Slavs and win the c-file every time. It is the entire content of the variation.
stages.mistake: Treating the Exchange Slav as an automatic draw. Black has scored well in it for a century by outplaying opponents who relaxed.
stages.ready: You can explain what the a4-pawn costs White.

stages.goal: Learn the freeing breaks and when to use them.
learn: The ...c5 break, which turns your solid position into an active one. It is the goal of nearly every Slav plan.
The ...e5 break, available when White's pieces drift to the queenside.
How to meet e4: usually ...Bg6 and then hit the centre with ...c5, rather than blocking with ...e5 immediately.
stages.drill: In ten games, count how many moves it takes you to achieve ...c5. Under fifteen is good; over twenty means you were too passive.
stages.mistake: Never breaking. A Slav that never plays ...c5 or ...e5 is just a cramped position with no weaknesses and no future.
stages.ready: You reach ...c5 or ...e5 in most of your games under good circumstances.

stages.goal: Take on the Semi-Slav and the theoretical monsters.
learn: The Meran, where you get a queenside majority and enormous complications.
The Botvinnik and Anti-Moscow gambits — among the sharpest lines in all of chess theory, and unavoidable if you play 4...e6.
Slav endgames with a queenside majority: how to create the outside passed pawn.
stages.drill: Decide honestly whether you want the Botvinnik. If not, choose the Moscow Variation move order and avoid it entirely.
stages.mistake: Drifting into the Semi-Slav without preparation. It is a completely different opening from the Main Line Slav.
stages.ready: You have chosen your branch and know it fifteen moves deep.

progression.study: Viswanathan Anand and Vladimir Kramnik played the defining Semi-Slav battles of the 2000s. For the classical Main Line, look at Max Euwe and Anatoly Karpov.
progression.next: Add the Queen's Gambit Declined as a second option. Between the Slav and the QGD you have an answer to every 1.d4 system White can build.
